item.title: Bose Brought Back Wired Earbuds After 11 Years. With ANC. For $99.
item.description:
Bose spent the last decade convincing people they didn't need cables. Now they're selling them again.

The Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds are exactly what the name promises: wired earbuds with active noise cancellation, USB-C connectivity, and no battery to charge. They're priced at $99, available for preorder now, and ship October 15.

This is Bose's first wired earbud in 11 years. The company discontinued its last wired model back in 2015, right as the industry was sprinting toward true wireless everything. The timing of this return isn't random. Multiple reports cite double-digit growth in wired earbud sales through 2025 and into 2026, driven largely by younger buyers who either never lived through the tangled-cable era or don't care.

What makes these interesting isn't nostalgia. It's the engineering. Traditional wired ANC earbuds, like Bose's own QC20 from 2013, needed a bulky battery pack clipped to the cable. These don't. The Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds pull power directly from the USB-C port on your phone, tablet, or laptop. No internal battery. No charging case. No degraded lithium cells three years from now.

The ANC itself uses Bose's QuietControl technology with four microphones, two per earbud, to monitor and cancel ambient sound. You get three modes: Quiet for full ANC, Aware for transparency, and Off for passive listening. All controlled from a button on the cable, not an app, because there is no app.

Audio runs through USB Audio Class 2, which means the earbuds accept lossless input at any sample rate and bit depth, then output at a fixed 24-bit/48kHz. That's higher resolution than most streaming services deliver and better than Bluetooth can manage without codec gymnastics. The wired connection also means zero latency, which matters for video calls, gaming, or any situation where lip sync drift is annoying.

The cable is 4.2 feet long. You get three sizes of silicone eartips, medium and large stability wings, an IPX4 splash rating, and a carry case. It ships in Black, White Smoke, and a limited Dewdrop Mint color.

The obvious compromise is the cable itself. You're tethered to your device, which means no walking away from your desk mid-call and a higher chance of snagging the cord on a door handle. But for $99, you're getting QuietControl ANC in a package that never needs charging and won't be e-waste in five years when the battery dies. That's a third the price of Bose's QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds, which cost $299 and will eventually stop holding a charge.

Bose is betting there's a market for people who'd rather plug in than charge up. Based on the wired earbud sales trajectory, they might be right.

item.title: Google's Fitbit Air Launches in India. The Price Is the Problem.
item.description:
Google just launched the Fitbit Air in India, and the whole point was supposed to be accessibility. A stripped-down fitness tracker for people who don't need GPS, don't want to pay for premium features, and just want step counts and sleep data that sync to their phone. Clean concept. But Google priced it in a way that might keep it from finding the audience it was designed for.

The Fitbit Air is Google's attempt to go truly budget in a market where Xiaomi and Realme own the entry-level wearables category. No always-on display, no onboard GPS, no altimeter. What you get is continuous heart rate monitoring, basic sleep tracking, smartphone notifications, and roughly seven days of battery life. It's lighter than the Charge series, uses a simpler band mechanism, and skips the color screen in favor of a monochrome OLED that's easier to read in direct sunlight but feels like a step back if you've used anything recent.

The pitch makes sense. India is one of the biggest wearables markets in the world, and the sub-$50 segment is where the volume lives. Brands like Noise, boAt, and Fire-Boltt have flooded that space with trackers that cost less than dinner and do just enough to justify wearing them. Google needed something that could compete on price while still carrying the Fitbit name and the Google Health integration that actually works.

But here's where it falls apart: Google is asking too much. Early reports suggest the Fitbit Air is priced higher than comparable local options that offer similar specs and, in some cases, better displays. The Fitbit app is more polished, the data accuracy is likely better, and you're buying into an ecosystem that connects to Google Fit and works across Android and iOS. But in a market this price-sensitive, "better software" doesn't move units the way a lower sticker price does.

Google has a history of misjudging what budget actually means. The Pixel A-series keeps inching up in price. The Nest Mini launched higher than the Echo Dot. And now the Fitbit Air arrives in India with a premium that doesn't match the product's intentionally limited feature set. If the goal was market share, the price needed to be aggressive. If the goal was margin, they should have added the features to justify it.

The Fitbit Air will find buyers—people who want the Google Health connection, existing Fitbit users stepping down from a Charge or Versa, and anyone who values data accuracy over flashy specs. But in a country where wearables are impulse buys and brand loyalty is thin, Google just made it harder for itself. Again.

item.title: Twelve South AirFly Drive Cuts the Cable From CarPlay for $40
item.description:
Twelve South just launched the AirFly Drive, a $40 dongle that converts your car's wired CarPlay or Android Auto connection into a wireless one. It's available now in black or white, and it does exactly one thing: lets you walk into your car and have CarPlay start automatically, no cable required.

The pitch is simple. Millions of cars shipped with CarPlay or Android Auto built in, but without the wireless version—either because the car predates it or because the wireless upgrade was bundled into a pricier trim package. The AirFly Drive is a compact aluminum cube that plugs into your car's USB port and stays there. Pair your iPhone once, and it auto-connects every time you start the car. No app, no account, no charging.

Twelve South says it works with more than 75 makes and model years going back to 2014, as long as your car has factory-wired CarPlay or Android Auto. The box includes both USB-A and USB-C adapters, so it should fit most data ports. There's a button on the device that lets you one-press switch between two paired phones, which is useful if you share the vehicle.

The company built its reputation on the original AirFly, a Bluetooth transmitter that let you use AirPods with airplane seatback screens and gym treadmills. That device became the top-selling Bluetooth adapter on Amazon. The AirFly Drive applies the same thinking to a different annoyance: the tangle of Lightning or USB-C cables draped across your center console.

Wireless CarPlay adapters aren't new. Amazon is full of them, many from brands you've never heard of, with wildly inconsistent reviews. What Twelve South brings is a known name and a track record of devices that actually work as advertised. The trade-off is size—the AirFly Drive is noticeably bulkier than some stick-style competitors.

The device is designed to stay plugged in permanently, which means it needs to handle heat and maintain a stable connection without your intervention. Twelve South says it's engineered to stay cool and promises ongoing compatibility updates as new phones and vehicle software ship.

At $40, it's cheaper than buying a new head unit and drastically cheaper than trading up to a newer car with wireless CarPlay built in. If your current routine involves fishing a cable out of the cupholder every single time you drive, that's probably worth it. The AirFly Drive is available now from Twelve South's website, with Amazon availability coming next week.

item.title: Amazon's Kindle Click Is a $35 Remote for People Who Read Under Blankets
item.description:
Amazon just announced a small Bluetooth remote that does one thing: turn pages on your Kindle. It's called the Kindle Click, it costs $34.99, and it's the kind of accessory that sounds ridiculous until you realize you've been propping your Kindle against a pillow with one hand while trying to tap the screen with a cold finger sticking out from under the covers.

The Click is a compact wireless remote that works with any Kindle from 2024 or later, including the newly redesigned Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and Kindle Colorsoft models Amazon also announced this week. It connects via Bluetooth, which means you can toss it in your bag, use it on a treadmill, or click through pages on a plane without having to reach over your tray table.

Amazon is also selling a more integrated option: a $79.99 magnetic Page-Turn Cover that snaps onto the new Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft Signature Editions. That case uses pogo pin connectivity and has physical page-turn buttons built into the cover itself. It's a spiritual successor to the discontinued Kindle Oasis, which had physical buttons and a cult following among people who never wanted to touch a screen.

But the Click is the more versatile accessory here. It works across Amazon's entire recent lineup, from the $149.99 entry-level Kindle all the way up to the $319.99 Colorsoft Signature Edition. That broader compatibility makes it a better long-term investment, especially if you upgrade devices every few years.

The new Kindle lineup itself got thinner, lighter, and more colorful. The Paperwhite now has a 7-inch display with what Amazon claims is the highest contrast ratio yet, plus 12 weeks of battery life. The Colorsoft is essentially a color version of the Paperwhite, with improved clarity and more even lighting thanks to nitride LEDs and custom display waveforms. Both launch October 28, while the base Kindle is available now.

But the Click is what stands out. Amazon figured out that the problem with e-readers isn't the screen or the battery or the resolution. It's that sometimes you just want to turn a page without moving your hand. Thirty-five dollars for that convenience? For some people, that's exactly the upgrade they didn't know they needed.

item.title: Apple Confirms iPhone 18 Pro Max Needs Hardware Swap for AT&T Bug
item.description:
Apple confirmed today that [iPhone 18 Pro Max](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=iPhone+18+Pro+Max&tag=techtreck02-20) owners experiencing cellular service issues on AT&T will need to replace their devices entirely. Software won't fix this one.

The $1,299 flagship has been plagued by connectivity problems since its September 18 launch. Thousands of users across the Apple Support Community, Reddit, and MacRumors Forums have reported their phones dropping into SOS mode, unable to make calls, send texts, or access data on AT&T's network. For two weeks, the cause remained unclear and Apple stayed silent.

That changed this afternoon. Apple released a statement acknowledging the issue affects a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max devices on AT&T's network. The company pushed iOS 27.0.1 earlier this week and an AT&T carrier settings update today, but those updates won't restore service to phones already affected. They're meant to prevent the problem from hitting more devices going forward.

If your iPhone 18 Pro Max already lost service, you're looking at a trip to the Apple Store or AT&T location for a hardware replacement. Apple is offering free swaps, but there's no formal service program yet.

The timing and scope point to something deeper than a software glitch. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is the only model in Apple's current lineup that uses a Qualcomm Snapdragon X80 modem in the United States. The smaller iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo both use Apple's custom C2 modem worldwide, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max uses the C2 in every other country. Only the U.S. iPhone 18 Pro Max got the Qualcomm chip, and only that model is experiencing these issues.

Apple hasn't confirmed whether the modem is the culprit, but the pattern is hard to ignore. The company spent years developing its own modem specifically to end its dependence on Qualcomm. The C2 debuted in this generation across most of the iPhone lineup. But for the Pro Max in the U.S. market, Apple stuck with Qualcomm's hardware. Now that decision is creating the kind of mess Apple usually avoids: a hardware defect affecting a flagship product weeks after launch, with no fix beyond swapping out the entire device.

AT&T sent text messages to customers yesterday telling them to update to iOS 27.0.1 immediately, warning that some phones may be unable to complete calls to 911. But users who installed the update reported it changed nothing. An internal AT&T email later clarified the update was meant to mitigate future impacts, not fix phones already broken.

If you're on AT&T with an iPhone 18 Pro Max and haven't experienced problems yet, install iOS 27.0.1 and the carrier update. If your phone already dropped service, book a Genius Bar appointment. And if you're shopping for an iPhone 18 Pro Max right now on AT&T, you might want to see how this plays out first.

item.title: Sony Quietly Redesigned the PS5 Slim. You Can't Tell From the Box.
item.description:
Sony slipped a major hardware revision into the PS5 Slim sometime in September 2026, and the only way you'd know is by cracking one open. Console technician Modyfikator89 tore down a Wolverine Limited Edition PS5 Slim and found a completely redesigned interior bearing a new EDM-051 motherboard, PS5 Pro-style cooling improvements, and a user-replaceable CMOS battery. Sony mentioned none of this in any announcement, didn't update the manual, and left the box completely unmarked.

The biggest practical change is the CMOS battery. On every PS5 Slim until now, swapping the CR2032 cell required removing the heatsink and dealing with the liquid metal thermal interface underneath. That's not something most people want to attempt at home. The new revision moves the battery to an accessible position behind a single screw, matching the approach Sony took with the PS5 Pro. CMOS batteries can last years, but they do eventually die, and when they do, you want the swap to be simple.

The cooling system got reworked too. The liquid metal containment around the APU now looks closer to the PS5 Pro design, with less surface area exposed directly to the thermal compound and better control around the processor. The heatsink itself uses different materials and construction compared to earlier Slim models. Sony has quietly tweaked PS5 cooling multiple times since launch, and this appears to be another step in refining thermal management and preventing the liquid metal leaks that plagued some early units.

The motherboard layout has been simplified overall, with components rearranged in ways that suggest Sony is still optimizing manufacturing. None of these changes affect gaming performance. This isn't a spec bump. It's about reliability, repairability, and long-term serviceability.

The frustrating part is that there's no way to know which revision you're buying. The Wolverine bundle shipped on September 15 at $649.99, and at least some of those units contain the new hardware. But Sony has a long history of rolling out silent revisions across the PS5 line without updating model numbers, packaging, or documentation. Two identical-looking PS5 Slim boxes sitting on a store shelf could contain meaningfully different internals, and you won't know until you're past the return window and someone pops the cover off years from now to replace a dead battery.

If you're buying a PS5 Slim today, you might get the new revision. You might not. Sony isn't saying, and that's the problem.

item.title: Google Pixel 10a Just Jumped to $599. The Same Phone, $100 More.
item.description:
Google raised the price of the Pixel 10a by $100 overnight. The phone that launched in March for $499 now costs $599 for the base 128GB model, with the 256GB variant climbing to $699. The new pricing is already live at the Google Store, Amazon, and Best Buy.

The timing is rough. Samsung raised prices on some Galaxy S26 models just yesterday. Now Google follows with its own hike, citing rising component costs—specifically memory. The company had warned this was coming. Back in August, Google VP Shakil Barkat told reporters the company had shielded consumers from supply fluctuations as long as possible, but the economics had fundamentally shifted.

What makes the increase particularly hard to swallow is what you're actually paying more for. The Pixel 10a still runs the Tensor G4 processor, the same chip that debuted with the Pixel 9 series back in 2024. That's a two-generation-old chipset at this point. Google did add upgraded wireless charging and satellite connectivity compared to the Pixel 9a, but the core experience is largely unchanged.

At $499, the Pixel 10a was a solid value proposition—Google's AI features, a capable camera system, seven years of software updates, and a clean Android experience in a phone made with recycled materials. At $599, that value equation shifts. You're now $100 away from flagship territory, where phones with current-generation silicon and more premium builds start appearing.

The international pricing follows the same pattern. The Pixel 10a now costs £599 in the UK, €649 in Europe, and $849 in Canada. All represent the same $100 equivalent increase.

Google isn't alone in this. Memory costs have been climbing across the industry, and phone makers are passing those increases directly to consumers. But when you're asking people to pay more for the same hardware they could have bought months ago at a lower price, the value proposition gets harder to defend. The Pixel 10a is still a capable phone. It's just not the deal it used to be.

item.title: Neurable One Puts EEG Brain Sensors in $499 Headphones. Again.
item.description:
Neurable wants you to know when your brain is tired before you do. The company just launched Neurable One, its third pair of EEG-equipped headphones, this time built entirely in-house instead of bolted onto someone else's hardware. It's available today for $499.

That's the same price Neurable charged for last year's MW75 Neuro LT, the lighter follow-up to its original $699 collaboration with Master & Dynamic. But the Neurable One isn't just a rebranded sequel. The company designed these from scratch, which means it finally controls the whole stack: 12 fabric EEG sensors sewn into the ear pads, 40mm beryllium drivers, six-microphone ANC, and the algorithms that try to make sense of your brainwaves while you work, rest, or doom-scroll.

The pitch is familiar. The headphones track your focus in real time, then nudge you to take a break when your attention starts to crater. But Neurable One adds two new metrics: capacity, which estimates how much more you can focus before burnout hits, and alpha peak frequency, a long-term brain health marker that drops as you age. The second one requires weeks of passive data collection, so it's less a daily dashboard and more of a longitudinal commitment.

Battery life sits at 22 hours with EEG off, 12 hours with brain tracking active. That's competitive with the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra, which both cost around the same but lack the neural monitoring party trick. Whether dry EEG sensors in headphones can deliver clinically useful data is still an open question. Researchers have noted that dry electrode systems are inherently noisy, and real-time feedback based on that signal risks overpromising.

But Neurable isn't selling medical devices. It's selling the promise that you can optimize your workday by listening to your brain instead of just your calendar. At $499, you're paying premium-headphone prices for that experiment. The audio hardware is solid enough to justify the cost on its own, but the EEG is the reason you'd pick these over anything else at this price. If you're curious whether your brain has been trying to tell you something, Neurable One is now shipping in the US.

item.title: Vivo X Fold 6 Finally Ships Global. The Battery Got Worse.
item.description:
Vivo's X Fold 6 just became the company's first foldable to ship outside China. Four months after its June launch in its home market, the phone is now available globally—starting in Europe at €2,199. That's roughly $2,400. For context, the same 12GB/512GB configuration sold for 8,999 yuan in China, which converts to about $1,342. The markup is 64%.

That's not the only downgrade. The global version also ships with a 6,900mAh battery instead of the 7,000mAh cell in the Chinese model. It's a small trim—probably a difference in how rated versus typical capacity gets listed—but it's still technically less. And unlike the Chinese launch, which offered four memory configurations (up to 16GB RAM and 1TB storage) and three colors, Europe gets exactly one option: 12GB/512GB in Horizon Blue. Take it or leave it.

The rest of the spec sheet stayed intact, and it's legitimately competitive. The X Fold 6 runs MediaTek's Dimensity 9500 Super Edition chip, features an 8.02-inch internal AMOLED display and a 6.51-inch cover screen (both 120Hz), and packs a ZEISS-tuned triple camera: 200MP main sensor, 50MP periscope telephoto with 3x optical zoom, and 50MP ultrawide. Charging hits 80W wired and 40W wireless. The phone weighs 228 grams and measures 4.4mm thick when unfolded.

That 200MP camera and sub-5mm thinness are rare in the foldable space. So is a battery north of 6,500mAh. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, which costs the same €2,199 in Germany for a 12GB/256GB model, ships with half the storage and a much smaller battery. Vivo's advantage is hardware. Its disadvantage is software maturity, retail presence, and the fact that most buyers outside China have never heard of the X Fold series.

This is also Vivo's first real test of whether a specs-first strategy works in markets where Samsung and Apple dominate mindshare. The X Fold 5 never left China. The X Fold 6 is betting that camera megapixels, battery capacity, and thinness matter more than brand recognition. Whether that's true depends on how many people are willing to spend flagship money on a company that's been invisible in foldables until now.

The phone is available now in Europe through Vivo's official store. No word yet on availability in other regions, though India was reportedly scheduled for an October 6 launch.

item.title: Amazon's Fire TV Stick 4K Gets a Remote You Can Navigate Blind
item.description:
Amazon just launched a new Fire TV Stick 4K, and the remote redesign is the part that actually matters.

The new Fire TV Remote has an asymmetric shape with a flat top and weighted, curved bottom, so you can tell which way you're holding it without flipping it over like a deck of cards in the dark. The home button gets its own metal surface, other controls are indented or distinctly shaped, and there's a customizable star button that can launch an app or toggle settings like closed captions. That last feature used to be reserved for Amazon's premium remotes.

The idea is simple: you shouldn't need to look at the remote to pause Netflix. It's a small tweak that solves a real problem, and Amazon says the new remote works with all Fire TV devices dating back to 2019.

The stick itself also got faster. Amazon claims apps launch over 35 percent faster and content starts playing nearly 20 percent faster than a similarly priced 4K streaming stick from another leading brand. It runs on a quad-core 1.7GHz processor, has 8GB of storage, and supports Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.3, 4K at 60fps, and HDR10 plus HDR10+. It ships with Vega OS, Amazon's newer operating system, which now supports over 2,000 apps including Spotify, Xbox, VLC, and the usual streaming suspects.

One thing it doesn't support: Dolby Vision. And sideloading apps is no longer an option on Vega OS, which will frustrate the tinkerers who like to customize their Fire TV experience.

The new Fire TV Stick 4K costs $59.99 and ships today in the US and UK. If you just want the redesigned remote for your existing Fire TV setup, it's available for pre-order at $14.99 and ships in late October. Amazon is also planning a Fire TV Remote Plus with aluminum housing, backlit buttons, and a Find My Remote feature for early 2027.

The remote redesign is overdue. Most streaming remotes are identical black rectangles that disappear into couch cushions and require a phone flashlight to operate. Amazon figured out that shape and texture matter as much as button layout. That's the story.

item.title: Garmin Cirqa Puts a $200 Price on What Whoop Charges You Forever
item.description:
Garmin just launched a screenless fitness band that looks almost exactly like a Whoop, tracks nearly everything a Whoop tracks, and costs $199.99. Once. No monthly fee, no annual subscription, no unlock-the-features-you-already-paid-for tax.

The Garmin Cirqa is a fabric-wrapped health tracker with no display, one button, and a ten-day battery. It monitors heart rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, sleep stages, stress, and recovery around the clock. It syncs to the Garmin Connect app over Bluetooth, supports over 80 activity types via connected GPS, and delivers metrics like VO2 max, HRV status, training readiness, and Body Battery.

That feature set puts it squarely against the Whoop 5.0, which requires a membership that runs between $199 and $359 per year depending on commitment length. Buy the Cirqa once and you own it. Garmin does offer an optional Connect+ subscription for $6.99 a month if you want extras like nutrition tracking and advanced coaching, but the core health and fitness data is yours without a recurring charge.

The band itself weighs about 21 grams with the strap, measures 47mm long and 9mm thick, and can be worn on the wrist or upper arm. It's swim-rated to 5 ATM, charges via a proprietary plug, and comes in four colors: black, French Gray, berry, and navy. Both small/medium and large/extra-large sizes cost the same $199.99.

Garmin is positioning the Cirqa as a complement to its watches, not a replacement. If you already own a Fenix or Forerunner, the Cirqa fills in 24/7 health data when you're not wearing your watch, and everything syncs back via TrueUp. If you don't own a Garmin watch, the Cirqa works standalone as a capable fitness tracker that lives entirely in the app.

The pitch is blunt: pay once, track forever. In a category where Whoop pioneered the hardware-as-service model and others followed, Garmin is betting that enough people would rather own their tracker outright. The Cirqa became available on July 24 directly from Garmin and works with iOS and Android.

Whether this kills the subscription model is doubtful. Whoop has built a devoted user base around its coaching and community features. But for anyone who wants continuous health tracking without a recurring bill, Garmin just handed you an out.

item.title: Sennheiser Put Replaceable Batteries in $300 Earbuds. That's the Whole Point.
item.description:
Sennheiser just did something no other major earbud maker has done: made the batteries replaceable. The Momentum True Wireless 5 earbuds, which started shipping in early September for $299.95, let you swap out the lithium-ion cells in both the earbuds and the charging case using a Phillips PH000 screwdriver. Sennheiser even throws the tool in the box.

This matters because battery degradation is what kills premium earbuds. The drivers, Bluetooth chipsets, and microphones can outlast the tiny cells powering them by years, but once capacity fades below a usable threshold, you're stuck buying a new pair or living with 90-minute listening sessions. Sennheiser is betting that buyers willing to spend $300 on earbuds also want them to last longer than 18 months.

The company claims up to 12 hours per charge with ANC off, six hours with it on, and 40 hours total with the case. That matches or beats most flagship competitors at launch, but the real value proposition kicks in two or three years down the road when you can order replacement cells instead of shopping for a new pair.

There's a catch, though: Sennheiser hasn't announced replacement battery pricing, SKUs, or where you'll actually buy them. The company also hasn't published a step-by-step repair guide or clarified whether DIY battery swaps void the one-year warranty. So while the hardware supports user replacement, the full ecosystem isn't there yet.

The rest of the spec sheet is flagship-grade but unsurprising. You get Bluetooth 6.0, aptX Lossless, Snapdragon Sound, 7mm TrueResponse drivers made in Ireland, adaptive ANC, Dolby Atmos with head tracking, and IP54 splash resistance. Five colors: Graphite, Cream, Copper, Denim, and Lavender. Qi wireless charging on the case. An 8-minute quick charge buys you an hour of playback.

None of that is new. What's new is Sennheiser treating a $300 product like something that should last. Marshall and Sennheiser's own over-ear Momentum 5 Wireless already have swappable batteries, but this is the first time a major brand has brought the concept to true wireless earbuds at scale. If replacement batteries actually show up for sale at reasonable prices, it changes the cost-per-year math in a way that matters more than another codec or another decibel of ANC.

The Momentum True Wireless 5 is available now through Sennheiser's site and select retailers. Whether it's the start of a repairability trend or a one-off experiment depends entirely on how many people are willing to pay for longevity they can't yet fully verify.

item.title: Apple's HomePad Launches October 13. The Price Is Still the Problem.
item.description:
Apple is finally ready to talk about its smart home hub. According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, the company will announce the long-rumored device on October 13, just three days before iPhone Duo pre-orders open and well ahead of the foldable phone's October 23 ship date.

The hub, which press outlets have been calling HomePad though Apple hasn't confirmed the name, will be joined by a refreshed HomePod mini and an upgraded Apple TV. All three are built around the rebuilt Siri AI that shipped with Apple's latest operating systems this year. That's what delayed the whole thing: the hardware was ready as far back as 2025, but Siri wasn't.

The HomePad itself reportedly features a 6-inch touchscreen that's about as thick as an iPhone, surrounded by chunky black bezels that look like they came off an older iPad. One version sits on a half-dome speaker base that evokes the sunflower iMac G4, a nostalgic design choice that feels very Apple. A second version is designed for wall mounting, with a thin square base that houses the speakers and microphones. That one stays plugged in via USB-C, which means dangling cables unless you've got in-wall power.

The device will run a new operating system blending elements of iOS, watchOS, and tvOS, with support for FaceTime calls, music playback, video streaming, and smart home controls for HomeKit-compatible devices. Voice and facial recognition will let the hub identify who's speaking, personalizing responses for different household members.

But here's the tension: nobody knows what Apple will charge. The figure floating around is roughly $350, pulled from a single Bloomberg report last October and repeated everywhere since without independent confirmation. If that holds, the HomePad would cost more than most Echo Show and Nest Hub models, which already work with far more third-party devices. The original HomePod launched at $349 in 2018, dropped to $299 within 14 months, and was discontinued by 2021.

Apple clearly thinks Siri AI is the differentiator, and maybe it is. But until October 13, we won't know if the rebuilt assistant feels quick enough to justify putting a screen on a speaker that costs as much as an iPad.

item.title: Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra Switches to MediaTek. That's Not the Problem.
item.description:
Samsung officially unveiled the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra today, and it ships October 7 with a notable shift under the hood: MediaTek's Dimensity 9500 chip replaces the Snapdragon silicon that powered previous generations. It's Samsung's clearest signal yet that MediaTek has arrived as a credible premium player. But the processor swap isn't the story.

The real question is whether $1,399 buys enough tablet to justify that price.

The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra packs a 14.6-inch OLED display running at 120Hz with a 2960 × 1848 resolution, an 11,600mAh battery with 45W fast charging, and up to 16GB of RAM with 1TB of storage in the top configuration. Samsung promises seven years of OS and security updates, which puts it ahead of nearly every Android competitor on long-term support. The tablet includes an S Pen, IP68 water and dust resistance, and a four-channel speaker system with spatial audio. It's running Android 17 with OneUI 9, complete with Samsung's latest Galaxy AI features and a three-section multi-window layout.

On paper, it's comprehensive. In practice, the upgrades over the Tab S11 Ultra feel incremental. The design is nearly identical, with the same ultra-slim 5.1mm profile. The battery capacity hasn't changed. The dual rear camera setup—13MP primary, 8MP ultrawide—and 12MP front camera are carryovers. Even the display specs remain static.

What's new is the Dimensity 9500, and Samsung's betting that its performance gains justify the unchanged (or slightly higher, depending on region) pricing. The chip supports Bluetooth 6.0 and Wi-Fi 7, future-proofing connectivity, and early benchmarks suggest it's competitive with Qualcomm's latest.

But here's the tension: at $1,399 for the base 12GB/256GB model—$1,599 for 512GB, $1,999 for the 1TB variant with 16GB RAM—the Tab S12 Ultra is asking iPad Pro money for an Android tablet in a market where Apple still owns the premium productivity narrative.

Samsung's advantage remains DeX mode, S Pen integration, and the flexibility of Android's file system. If you live in Samsung's ecosystem and need a serious productivity tablet with a proper pointing device and desktop-class multitasking, the Tab S12 Ultra is still the best Android option available. The seven-year update promise alone sets a new standard.

But calling this an essential upgrade from the S11 Ultra requires squinting past the spec sheet. Samsung held the line on design, display, and battery while swapping the processor and raising the floor price. That's a hard sell when the previous generation is about to get very attractive on the secondary market.

The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra goes on sale October 7 in Gray and Silver. Pre-orders are likely live in select markets today.

item.title: Sony's WH-1000XM6 Gets Sand Pink. That's Not Why It Matters.
item.description:
Sony released a Sand Pink colorway for the WH-1000XM6 over-ear headphones in February, joining the existing Black, Platinum Silver, and Midnight Blue options. It costs $459.99, ten dollars more than the other colors for reasons Sony hasn't bothered to explain.

The new shade is nice enough—a muted peachy tone that splits the difference between millennial pink and actual sand—but the more interesting story is buried underneath the press photos. The WH-1000XM6, which launched last May at $449.99, has quietly become the default premium headphone recommendation despite a $50 price bump over its predecessor.

That's partly because Sony brought back the folding hinge that the XM5 controversially ditched, making the XM6 both more portable and more practical than the model it replaced. But it's also because the competition hasn't kept pace. The Sonos Ace Ultra costs the same and sounds excellent, but it's locked into Sonos's ecosystem in ways that matter if you don't already own Sonos speakers. Bose's QuietComfort Ultra Headphones run $449 in the UK but feel iterative rather than essential.

The XM6 improved noise cancellation over an already class-leading predecessor, added Bluetooth 5.3 support, and kept the 30-hour battery life that makes daily charging unnecessary. Sony also upgraded to a QN3 processor that's seven times faster than the chip in the XM5, though most of that speed goes toward better ANC algorithms rather than features you'll consciously notice.

The Sand Pink model doesn't change any of that. It's the same headphones in a different finish, available now through Sony's website and major retailers. The premium over the standard colors is annoying but small enough that it probably won't matter to anyone who's already decided they want pink headphones.

What does matter is that Sony's managed to raise the price, eliminate color parity, and still produce the safest recommendation in the category. That's the kind of market position that lets you charge an extra ten bucks for paint.

item.title: iPhone Duo Pre-Orders Open October 16. Here's What Apple Isn't Saying.
item.description:
Apple announced its first foldable iPhone at its September event, and then promptly went quiet on the things people actually want to know. The iPhone Duo ships October 23, with pre-orders opening October 16, starting at $1,999. That part's clear. What's not clear is almost everything else.

The device uses two screens connected by a continuous frame, creating what Apple calls a fluid transition between open and closed states. When fully open, it's the thinnest iPhone Apple's ever made. The two halves share the same aspect ratio across both displays, which is a different approach than Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold series with its narrow outer screen.

But Apple skipped over crucial durability details. There's no mention of crease visibility, no water resistance rating announced, and no information about whether the displays use ultra-thin glass or plastic. These aren't minor spec-sheet details—they're the make-or-break questions that determine whether a $1,999 foldable lives in your pocket or a drawer after six months.

The other glaring omission: camera specs. Apple showed the Duo alongside the iPhone 18 Pro, which got a detailed camera walkthrough, but said almost nothing about what lenses the foldable actually has. One report notes the lack of a telephoto lens, which would be a strange choice at this price point, but Apple hasn't confirmed that either way.

The matte screen finish is confirmed, which should help with glare but might feel odd if you're used to the glossy panels on every other iPhone. And unlike the iPhone 18 Pro models that launched September 18, the Duo is coming a full month later—enough time for early reviews to surface, or for production issues to leak.

Apple's silence on durability is the most telling part. Every other manufacturer launching foldables leads with hinge cycles, screen protection layers, and warranty terms because those are the obvious concerns. Apple skipped all of it. That's either supreme confidence or a sign that the answers aren't ready yet.

The October 16 pre-order date gives Apple three more weeks to fill in the blanks. Until then, you're buying a $1,999 question mark with the thinnest chassis Apple's ever built and almost no concrete details about how long it'll stay that way.

item.title: Nothing's Headphone (1) Pro Puts a Studio Toggle Inside the Earcup
item.description:
Nothing just launched the Headphone (1) Pro, and buried among the spec-sheet upgrades is a feature that actually makes sense: a physical switch inside the left earcup that flips the sound profile to completely flat EQ. No app, no menu diving, just a toggle for when you need neutral sound.

The Pro model costs $399 and ships today at Nothing's site, Amazon, and Best Buy. That's $100 more than the original Headphone (1), which launched last summer at $299. For that premium you get a triple-driver setup instead of a single 40mm driver, 46dB of adaptive noise cancellation instead of the standard model's less aggressive ANC, and 10 microphones instead of six.

The triple-driver architecture is the real story here. Nothing split the frequency range across a 40mm dynamic driver for bass, a 13x8mm precision driver for mids, and an xMEMS solid-state driver for treble. Most flagship headphones from Sony, Bose, and Apple still use a single driver per earcup. Nothing worked with London's Metropolis Studios to tune the sound, and the Flat EQ switch is the centerpiece of that collaboration.

Inside the Nothing X app, you can independently adjust the main drivers and the precision driver, which gives you granular control over the sound signature. There are also five EQ presets from Metropolis Studios, plus spatial audio modes that simulate different listening environments like concert halls and live houses. Head tracking is optional.

Battery life is rated at 68 hours with ANC off and 30 hours with it on. Fast charging gives you two hours of playback after five minutes plugged in. The headphones support Bluetooth 6.1 with LDAC, plus USB-C for lossless audio and a 3.5mm jack for wired listening. The build uses aluminum for the frame, titanium for the cup holders, and scratch-resistant glass on the outside. They weigh 327 grams and come in black or white.

The question is whether the Pro model justifies the price jump. At $399, it's competing directly with the Sony WH-1000XM6, Bose QuietComfort Headphones, and Sennheiser MOMENTUM 5 Wireless. The triple-driver system and physical Flat EQ switch will appeal to anyone who cares about sound tuning, but most buyers prioritize comfort, ANC performance, and battery life over granular audio control. Nothing needs to prove the extra hardware is worth the ask, especially when the original Headphone (1) required significant EQ adjustments to sound its best.

The Headphone (1) Pro is available now at Nothing's website, Amazon, and Best Buy for $399.

item.title: Sonos Ace Ultra Ships Today at $449. The Ecosystem Is the Whole Point.
item.description:
The Sonos Ace Ultra is available today for $449, exactly two years after the original Ace arrived with the same price tag and a lot of unanswered questions. This time around, Sonos isn't just selling a pair of premium headphones. It's selling a node in your home audio network that happens to sit on your head.

The headline feature is Headphone Linking, which lets you pull audio from any Sonos speaker in your system directly to the Ace Ultra over Wi-Fi. Press the Content Key, and whatever's playing in the kitchen moves to your ears. That's the pitch Sony can't match with the WH-1000XM6, and it's why Sonos kept the price at $449 instead of undercutting its obvious rival.

The hardware upgrades are real but incremental. Sonos claims the active noise cancellation is twice as effective as the original Ace, thanks to deeper ear cups and a redesigned 10-microphone array. Battery life is up to 35 hours. There's an Aware mode for transparency, and the usual collection of EQ options and wear detection features you'd expect at this price.

But early reviews suggest Sonos still hasn't caught Sony or Bose on noise cancellation. Gizmodo's reviewer found the Ace Ultra middle-of-the-pack on a plane and subway, letting in more engine drone and train screech than the Bose QuietComfort Ultra or Sony WH-1000XM6. TechRadar gave Sony a slight edge in ANC testing, crediting the WH-1000XM6's 12-microphone system versus Sonos' 10. For a product positioned as premium, that gap matters.

The Ace Ultra doesn't have a headphone jack. Sonos includes a USB-C to 3.5mm cable in the box, which means you're carrying a dongle if you want wired listening. The company kept the black and white colorways from the original instead of expanding the palette, despite early rumors suggesting five options.

If you already own Sonos speakers, the Ace Ultra makes more sense than it does for everyone else. The ecosystem integration is genuinely differentiated, and 35 hours of battery is competitive. But if you're shopping purely on ANC performance or sound quality without the Sonos system to back it up, Sony's WH-1000XM6 remains the safer bet at the same $449 price point. Sonos built a compelling product for its existing users. Whether that's enough to pull people away from Sony is the real test.

item.title: Insta360 X6 Is the First 360 Camera That Actually Works at Night
item.description:
The 360 camera market has a problem: most models are great in daylight and mediocre at everything else. Battery dies mid-shoot. Low light turns footage into mush. Build quality feels like a compromise because you're buying two cameras duct-taped together.

Insta360's new X6 doesn't fix all of that, but it fixes enough to matter. According to early reviews, this is the first small 360 camera that can handle low-light shooting without turning your footage into a grainy mess, and it does it while lasting long enough to actually finish the job. That's a bigger deal than it sounds.

The X6 keeps the same basic form factor as previous Insta360 models but adds a more rugged build and what reviewers are calling pin-sharp image quality regardless of lighting conditions. One tester described it as the most capable small 360 camera they've used, which is notable given how crowded this category has become. The low-light performance is the real story here because 360 cameras have historically struggled the moment the sun goes down. Dual lenses mean each sensor gets less light than a traditional action cam, so most 360 footage shot indoors or at dusk looks like it was filmed through a screen door.

Battery life also got a meaningful bump. If you've ever tried to shoot 360 video on a long hike or a full day of travel, you know the format is a battery killer. Two lenses recording simultaneously at high resolution will do that. The X6 apparently lasts long enough that you're not constantly hunting for a charging cable, which makes it significantly more practical for actual use rather than quick demos.

Insta360 has been iterating on this design for years, and the X6 feels like the version where they finally solved the format's most annoying limitations rather than just adding megapixels or frame rates. The company hasn't published official pricing yet, but expect it to land somewhere in the typical action cam premium range given the dual-lens hardware and processing grunt required to stitch 360 footage in real time.

If you've written off 360 cameras because past models felt too compromised for serious use, the X6 might be worth a second look. It's still a niche format, but a niche format that now works in more than just perfect conditions.

item.title: Roku Built Its First OLED TVs. That's the Real Story.
item.description:
Roku just launched its first OLED televisions, and the significance isn't the panels themselves—it's that Roku, the company that built its reputation on affordably accessible streaming sticks and budget TVs, is now selling premium displays.

The new lineup includes two models: the Roku Pro Series OLED TV and the Roku Pro Series LX OLED TV. Both represent Roku's entry into high-performance display territory, a market segment the brand has historically left to Sony, LG, and Samsung while it focused on making streaming software ubiquitous and hardware cheap.

Roku's press materials position the launch as a response to growing demand for high-performance displays at approachable prices, which is corporate-speak for "OLED panels are finally cheap enough for us to build a competitive product." That's not criticism—it's smart timing. OLED pricing has dropped considerably over the past two years, and Roku's strength has always been knowing when a technology hits the sweet spot between capability and cost.

What's less clear is how Roku plans to differentiate these sets beyond the obvious streaming integration. Every TV ships with Roku's interface baked in at this point, either as a licensed platform or through an HDMI dongle. The real test will be whether Roku can deliver picture quality that justifies a premium over its budget line while undercutting the established OLED players on price.

The Pro Series LX OLED designation suggests a tiered approach—likely a higher-end model with additional features or a larger panel size—but specifics on resolution, refresh rates, HDR support, and crucially, pricing remain sparse. Without those details, it's hard to assess whether Roku is genuinely disrupting the OLED market or just adding another nameplate to a crowded field.

Still, the move signals a shift in Roku's strategy. The company built its business on being the software layer that sits on top of everyone else's hardware. Now it's betting it can compete on the hardware itself, in a category where brand loyalty runs deep and picture quality is ruthlessly scrutinized. It's a gamble, but if anyone knows how to turn commodity technology into a consumer hit, it's Roku.
